title: Biodiversity governance is expanding while species loss, forest decline, and ecosystem livelihood risks persist
source_unit: United Nations Statistics Division, Sustainable Development Goals Report 2026, Goal 15: Life on Land
geography: Global SDG indicator assessment across countries, ecosystems, species, forests, and biodiversity-governance systems

denominator.unit: global biodiversity indicator and country-policy frame

red_list_index.unit: approximate upper bound of the Red List Index in 2025, down from 0.80 in 1993

national_biodiversity_targets.unit: countries with national biodiversity targets established by 2025

environmental_accounting_countries.unit: countries implementing the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting in 2025

observations.method: UN SDG indicator synthesis drawing on the Red List Index, national biodiversity targets, and environmental-economic accounting systems.
observations.uncertainty: Species-risk indicators, national targets, and accounting adoption measure different objects and have uneven country coverage; policy adoption does not show ecological recovery or implementation quality.
observations.subgroup: Species, ecosystems, countries, Indigenous and local communities, conservation institutions, and populations dependent on ecosystem services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Growing biodiversity governance can produce meaningful protection and better measurement even while global extinction risk worsens due to lagged ecological response and persistent pressures.

denominator.unit: global forest area and annual forest-change estimates

forest_loss_since_2015.unit: million hectares of forest lost since 2015

forest_share_land.unit: percent of Earth's land covered by forests in 2025, down from 33.3 percent in 1990

deforestation_rate_2015_2025.unit: million hectares per year of deforestation during 2015-2025

forests_under_management_plans.unit: percent of total forest area under long-term management plans

observations.method: UN SDG synthesis of global forest-area, deforestation, forest-management, and protected-area data.
observations.uncertainty: Forest area, forest quality, management plans, and biodiversity outcomes are not interchangeable; global averages conceal regional loss, restoration, and land-use differences.
observations.subgroup: Forest-dependent communities, agricultural and livestock systems, forest managers, governments, biodiversity, water systems, and climate-vulnerable populations.
observations.counterinterpretation: Slowing deforestation and expanded management plans indicate policy capacity, but they may coexist with degradation, displacement of land-use pressure, and weak local rights.

denominator.unit: identified key biodiversity areas used in the UN assessment

average_kba_protection_2025.unit: percent average protected coverage of each key biodiversity area in 2025

average_kba_protection_2000.unit: percent average protected coverage of each key biodiversity area in 2000

protection_gap.value: many countries may have identified only a portion of their key biodiversity areas, potentially as little as half

regional_variation.value: average coverage exceeds 60 percent in Europe and Northern America but falls below 25 percent in parts of Oceania

observations.method: UN SDG comparison of key biodiversity area identification and protected/conserved-area overlap across ecosystems and regions.
observations.uncertainty: Site identification is incomplete and protection overlap does not establish effective management, ecological connectivity, or community consent.
observations.subgroup: Key biodiversity areas, protected-area authorities, local and Indigenous communities, conservation organizations, and regions with uneven mapping capacity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Formal protection can be a foundation for conservation, but unrecognized sites and weak enforcement mean legal coverage can overstate real security.

denominator.unit: warm-water reef-building coral and dependent-livelihood assessment

warm_water_corals_high_risk_2008.unit: percent of warm-water reef-building corals at high risk of extinction in 2008

warm_water_corals_high_risk_2025.unit: percent of warm-water reef-building corals at high risk of extinction in 2025

reef_dependent_livelihoods.unit: approximately millions of people relying on reefs for fisheries, tourism, coastal protection, and cultural values

compounding_pressures.value: climate change, pollution, and unsustainable fishing compound coral deterioration

observations.method: UN SDG synthesis of species-risk indicators and ecosystem-service livelihood dependencies.
observations.uncertainty: The livelihood estimate is broad and ecosystem dependence varies by location; coral-risk trends do not predict a uniform loss of fisheries, tourism, protection, or cultural value in every community.
observations.subgroup: Coastal communities, fishers, tourism workers, Indigenous peoples, small-island populations, coral ecosystems, and households dependent on coastal protection.
observations.counterinterpretation: Restoration, local stewardship, fisheries governance, and climate adaptation may protect some services even as global coral risk rises; benefits and losses are unevenly distributed.

related_sources.claim: UNEP GEO-7 provides a complementary integrated planetary-health and transformation scenario.
FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment 2025 provides complementary forest-area and management evidence.

boundary: This record adds a biodiversity-to-livelihoods and governance route linking species risk, forests, key biodiversity areas, coral ecosystems, conservation law, accounting, and dependent communities. It uses global SDG indicators and publication-level estimates, not individual livelihood histories, local ecological causal estimates, or proof that legal targets produce ecological recovery.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official UN SDG 2026 Goal 15 page was reviewed for species risk, biodiversity targets, accounting, forest loss and management, key biodiversity areas, coral risk, and livelihood-dependence figures.
